name: Emeka Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior software developer at a tech company scheduling lift maintenance visits, after a hardware shop closed and I earned a two-year college diploma. I use AI now and then to explain old code, but my lead still checks my changes before customers see a visit date. Leila, my partner, cleans hotel rooms, our children are grown, and lower pay leaves us renting with less than three weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the lift-maintenance team that a small AI tool might tidy the service calendar, but somebody still has to check whether a repair visit was booked for the right building. I sometimes use AI to explain a piece of old code, then run the calendar test myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, with a two-year college diploma, but still a junior and paid at the low end. My partner Leila cleans hotel rooms, our children are grown, and our rent and bills leave just under three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing booking-date bugs and show my lead the weekly list of missed visits. We would suspend the paid television package for six months and save 25 monthly if both wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious even without a big AI shift. A hotel can cut cleaning hours for ordinary reasons, and we do not have a long reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was a missed visit like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lift in one block needed an inspection on Tuesday, but the calendar sent the crew on Thursday. I found the date error in a test record before the notice went out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you do before coding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I stocked and sold parts in a hardware shop until it closed. I went to college because I liked keeping a stock list accurate. Writing code is harder than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking planning, booking, checking and coding will reach our lift calendar before it reaches the physical repair crew. I would ask the company to show a human review of safety-related visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The calendar fixes I do could be automated, and I might lose paid junior shifts. Leila’s hotel work is hands-on, but her wage alone will not cover our rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my lead for approved paid time to learn the AI scheduling test on invented lift visits, one hour each week. If approved, I’d compare its dates with the service rulebook; if my hours shrink, I’d search paid local building-service desk vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours, though I would rather test the tool than guess about it. A copied calendar entry can still strand someone in a broken lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the test catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enter a lift due for inspection after a public holiday and check whether the tool skips a required day. My lead would review the result before any real schedule changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for evening lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from less than three weeks of savings. I would take the approved paid hour or keep working without calling it training.

I want **paid AI testing** on invented schedules first.

I cannot rely on **hotel cleaning pay** alone for rent.

**Search paid service desks** if hours shrink and local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious** about own hours while testing changes.

fieldNote: His **new AI learning** uses invented visits and requires paid time plus lead review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write our service calendar code and make the safety checks too. Robots working on lift machinery and cleaning hotel rooms may follow around 2031, so our screen work changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could let its junior developers go, including me. We have less than three weeks saved, and Leila’s pay would not carry the rent while I wait for another software opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop the television package now and ask for written notice of any cuts. If my developer job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local hardware-store stock vacancies only if they exist and wages cover rent and food; I would ask my brother whether he can lend us a room only if rent cannot be met, without counting on his answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about the speed of losing my wage. The parts shelves are familiar, but I cannot pay rent with a memory of working in a hardware shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your brother take you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask only in a rent crisis, and he could say no. His household has its own space and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would stock work last after robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe only until physical robots arrive around 2031. I would take a paid opening if one existed, but I would not call it permanent.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach lift-calendar code and safety checking before physical repair work.
I expect **repair robots around 2031** to reach lift machinery and hotel cleaning later.
think: I expect my **junior developer wage** could end quickly.
I cannot count on **Leila or my brother** replacing my pay.
do: **Cancel television package** and seek written job-cut notice now.
**Apply for stock work** after 2028 loss only if local vacancies cover rent and food.
**Ask brother** about a room only in rent crisis, without assuming he can help.
feel: **Alarmed** about immediate rent after wage loss.
S2.quote: I cannot pay rent with a memory of working in a hardware shop.
fieldNote: Hardware stock is **familiar work**, but a paid vacancy is uncertain and robots may reach it around 2031.
Family help is **conditional on crisis**, never counted as current household income.

steps.text: Cancel paid television package when developer cuts threaten

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to learn which lift checks still need people on site. Robots for physical repair and hotel cleaning may arrive around 2034, later than the calendar code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know a little about parts from the old shop, but inspecting a lift is a different responsibility. I would only enter that trade through a paid apprenticeship with proper safety training, because our savings cannot fund unpaid months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the lift contractor this year about actual paid trainee vacancies and the safety certificate required. If it offers a paid apprenticeship that covers rent and bills, I’d enrol and complete the supervised inspection lessons; we would save 30 monthly only while both wages continue, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply only to paid local maintenance openings for which I qualify and whose wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my coding role, but I could make a measured choice with five years. A safety certificate has to mean I can inspect a real lift, not just fill a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check your inspection work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified lift technician would have to sign each inspection while I train. I would not sign a safety sheet on my own as a beginner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid trainee place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer wage while it exists and continue asking about openings. I would not take an unpaid course that leaves us short of rent.

I expect **repair robots around 2034** after code changes.

I need **qualified supervision** before a new trade can pay.

fieldNote: His **trade shift** depends on an actual paid opening and supervised safety learning.

steps.text: Enrol in paid lift apprenticeship only if vacancy covers bills and qualified technician supervises lessons
Save 30 monthly while both household wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2036 gives us time to check which safety duties still require a technician before the software takes over. Physical lift repair and hotel cleaning robots may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still need to earn at 68; I have no confirmed retirement figure and do not want to guess. If both wages last, we might build a few months of rent, but our cash cushion is thin today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing lift-calendar bugs while the developer role pays, and save 40 monthly only while both wages continue. I’d check the lift contractor’s paid trainee vacancies each year and enrol only if paid supervised training covers our bills; if my software role ends after 2036, I’d apply to a paid qualified maintenance opening only if I had completed safety training and its wage covered rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d still be anxious about our present cash, even with ten years to plan. I would rather know the cost of the next step than promise an easy retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no apprenticeship is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer role while it pays and reconsider maintenance when a paid trainee place appears. I would not describe myself as a lift inspector without supervised training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children be your retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and Leila and I need to make decisions from wages and figures we can verify.

I expect **lift robots around 2039** to follow later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because losing my junior developer wage would leave Leila unable to cover our rent alone. Written notice, a real paid local stock vacancy and a brother willing to help only in a rent crisis would matter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I already know how to inspect a lift. I do not. Selling parts is not the same as signing a safety sheet.

headlineQuote: Selling parts is not the same as signing a safety sheet.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, low pay and under three weeks saved.
He and Leila **rent** while their grown children support separate households.
He **uses AI occasionally** and checks lift schedules with his lead.
He considers **paid supervised lift training** only if a real trainee vacancy covers household bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior wage before another bill-covering job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid local stock work and conditional family help in a rent crisis would matter.
